claim: Too wide or too narrow generalization is linked to neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: However, too wide or too narrow generalization is linked to neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on neuropsychiatric disorders and generalization.

claim: Blocking dopamine D2-receptors (D2R) altered generalization behavior as revealed by an increased kurtosis of the generalization gradient.
source: Blocking dopamine D2-receptors (D2R) altered generalization behavior as revealed by an increased kurtosis of the generalization gradient, and a decreased width of model-derived generalization parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the pharmacological manipulation and behavioral measurements.

claim: D2R-blockade decreased the width of model-derived generalization parameters.
source: Blocking dopamine D2-receptors (D2R) altered generalization behavior as revealed by an increased kurtosis of the generalization gradient, and a decreased width of model-derived generalization parameters.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling of behavioral data.

claim: D2R-blockade modulated similarity-based responses in the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, D2R-blockade modulated similarity-based responses in the hippocampus and decreased midbrain-hippocampal connectivity, which in turn correlated with individual differences in generalization.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data showing changes in hippocampal activity.

claim: D2R-blockade decreased midbrain-hippocampal connectivity.
source: Moreover, D2R-blockade modulated similarity-based responses in the hippocampus and decreased midbrain-hippocampal connectivity, which in turn correlated with individual differences in generalization.
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis from fMRI data.

claim: Midbrain-hippocampal connectivity correlated with individual differences in generalization.
source: Moreover, D2R-blockade modulated similarity-based responses in the hippocampus and decreased midbrain-hippocampal connectivity, which in turn correlated with individual differences in generalization.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between connectivity measures and model parameters.

claim: Dopaminergic activity in the hippocampus may relate to the degree of generalization.
source: These results suggest that dopaminergic activity in the hippocampus may relate to the degree of generalization and highlight a potential target for treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing effects of D2R blockade on hippocampal activity and generalization behavior.

claim: Aberrant generalization is implicated in several neuropsychiatric diseases including schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, depression, and drug abuse.
source: Indeed, aberrant generalization is implicated in several neuropsychiatric diseases including schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, depression, and drug abuse (Dunsmoor and Paz, 2015; Gotlib and Joormann, 2010; Lissek et al., 2014b; Lucantonio et al., 2015; Moustafa et al., 2010; Shohamy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Two basic forms of generalization can be distinguished based on what constitutes the relation among stimuli: associative and stimulus generalization.
source: Two basic forms of generalization can be distinguished based on what constitutes the relation among stimuli; associative and stimulus generalization.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about types of generalization.

claim: In associative generalization, the associative relationship among stimuli determines similarity.
source: In the case of associative generalization, such as transitive inference and acquired equivalence, the associative relationship among stimuli determines similarity.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about associative generalization.

claim: In stimulus generalization, the relationship among stimuli is based on the similarity along one or more perceptual dimensions.
source: In contrast, in stimulus generalization the relationship among stimuli is based on the similarity along one or more perceptual dimensions (frequency of sounds, color, line orientation, etc.).
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about stimulus generalization.

claim: Early research suggested a role for dopamine in mediating generalization by demonstrating that blockade of dopamine receptors during generalization tests alters response gradients in rats and pigeons.
source: Early research suggested a role for dopamine in mediating generalization by demonstrating that blockade of dopamine receptors during generalization tests alters response gradients in rats and pigeons (Lyons et al., 1973a; 1973b; Terrace, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal research.

claim: Evidence from neuroimaging suggests that dopaminoceptive and dopaminergic regions such as the striatum and the midbrain are involved in generalization.
source: While the effects of dopamine have not been investigated in humans, evidence from neuroimaging suggests that dopaminoceptive and dopaminergic regions such as the striatum and the midbrain are involved in generalization (Kahnt et al., 2012; Wimmer et al., 2012; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: The hippocampus is thought to contribute to associative generalization by representing higher-order relationships among different stimuli.
source: Specifically, the hippocampus is thought to contribute to associative generalization by representing higher-order relationships among different stimuli (Eichenbaum, 1999; Howard et al., 2005; Kumaran and McClelland, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on hippocampal function.

claim: Human imaging and animal lesion studies suggest that the hippocampus may also be involved in similarity-based stimulus generalization not requiring inference.
source: However, human imaging and animal lesion studies suggest that the hippocampus may also be involved in similarity-based stimulus generalization not requiring inference (Casasola et al., 2007; Kahnt et al., 2012; Lissek et al., 2014a; Solomon and Moore, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous imaging and lesion studies.

claim: Subjects learned the discrimination within the first 50 trials and performed at high levels afterwards.
source: Subjects learned the discrimination within the first 50 trials and performed at high levels afterwards (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Performance increased as a function of time during discrimination training.
source: Performance increased as a function of time (two-way, group-by-time ANOVA, main effect of time, F(39,1716) = 18.98, P < 0.001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Performance during discrimination training did not differ between groups.
source: but did not differ between groups (main effect of group, F(1,44) = 0.41, P = 0.53; group-by-time interaction, F(39,1716) = 1.27, P = 0.13; two-way, group-by-CS type ANOVA, main effect of group, F(1,44) = 0.35, P = 0.56; group-by-CS type interaction, F(1,44) = 0.39, P = 0.53, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and Figure 2B.

claim: Learning-related activity in the ventral striatum did not differ between groups during discrimination training.
source: Moreover, learning-related activity in the ventral striatum (Delgado, 2007) did not differ between groups (see Figure 3)
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Responses during the generalization test described a bell-shaped gradient around the CS+ and revealed a peak shift.
source: Responses described a bell-shaped gradient around the CS+ and revealed a peak shift (Derenne, 2010; Purtle, 1973; Wisniewski et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and citations to previous research on peak shift.

claim: Average responding was stronger to orientations on the side of the CS+ that was farther away from the CS−.
source: Specifically, average responding was stronger to orientations on the side of the CS+ that was farther away from the CS− (paired t-test on responding to stimuli left vs. right of the CS+, t = 2.99, P = 0.006).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Peak shifts are typical for intradimensional discrimination with one CS+ and one CS− and are thought to result from the summation of excitatory and inhibitory gradients around the CS+ and CS−, respectively.
source: Such peak shifts are typical for intradimensional discrimination with one CS+ and one CS−; they are thought to result from the summation of excitatory and inhibitory gradients around the CS+ and CS−, respectively, and have been observed across many species and stimuli (Ghirlanda and Enquist, 2003; Pearce et al., 2008; Spence, 1937).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and established knowledge about peak shifts.

claim: The amisulpride group had a significantly greater kurtosis in their generalization gradient compared to the placebo group.
source: Accordingly, a test for differences in the kurtosis of group-specific distributions (Pearson type VII distribution, see Materials and methods) revealed a significantly greater kurtosis in the amisulpride group compared to placebo (PA: 6.73, PP: 3.29; permutation test, P = 0.043).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the shape of behavioral generalization gradients.

claim: Amisulpride narrowed the width and increased the peak of the behavioral generalization gradient.
source: This finding demonstrates that amisulpride narrowed the width and increased the peak of the behavioral generalization gradient, and suggests that D2R activity alters the neurocomputational processes that mechanistically control generalization behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the kurtosis analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The model with the Gaussian similarity function fitted the behavioral data better than the model with the exponential similarity function.
source: This was confirmed by a formal model comparison using the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC) (Gaussian: AIC = 9586.4, BIC = 9629.2; Exponential: AIC = 9691.6, BIC = 9734.4).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison statistics.

claim: Both Gaussian and exponential models predicted behavioral responses reliably.
source: Although both models predicted behavioral responses reliably (Gaussian: t = 11.06, P < 0.001; exponential: t = 11.38, P < 0.001)
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of model predictions against behavioral data.

claim: Regression coefficients were significantly higher for the Gaussian model compared to the exponential model.
source: we found significantly higher regression coefficients for the Gaussian model (paired t-test t = 5.34, P < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of regression coefficients.

claim: The model with group-specific parameters accurately reproduced responses in both groups, including the differences in the shape of the generalization gradients.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2D, the model (with group-specific parameters) accurately reproduced responses in both groups, including the differences in the shape of the generalization gradients.
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of Figure 2D and model fitting results.

claim: There was a significant group difference in the width of the excitatory generalization coefficient, with a smaller coefficient in the amisulpride group compared to the placebo group.
source: Notably, comparing the model parameters between groups (Table 1), revealed significant group differences in the width of the excitatory generalization coefficient, with a smaller coefficient in the amisulpride group compared to the placebo group (permutation test, P = 0.035).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters between groups.

claim: The width of the inhibitory coefficient was smaller in the amisulpride group, but this difference was not significant.
source: The width of the inhibitory coefficient was also smaller in the amisulpride group, but this difference was not significant (P = 0.069).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters between groups.

claim: The learning rate during test did not differ between groups.
source: Importantly, the learning rate during test did not differ between groups (P = 0.21), demonstrating that additional learning during the test session, which might have been altered by amisulpride, cannot account for the differences in generalization gradients.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters between groups.

claim: Individual estimates confirmed a significant difference in the width of the excitatory generalization coefficient between groups.
source: Comparing the resulting individual estimates between groups confirmed a significant difference in the width of the excitatory (two-sample t-test, t = -2.03, P = 0.024)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of individual model parameter estimates.

claim: Individual estimates showed a trend-level difference in the width of the inhibitory generalization coefficient between groups.
source: and to a lesser degree, the inhibitory generalization coefficient (t = -1.59, P = 0.059, Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of individual model parameter estimates shown in Figure 5.

claim: D2R blockade modulates the computational processes that control the width of stimulus generalization, resulting in narrower generalization.
source: These results suggest that D2R blockade modulates the computational processes that control the width of stimulus generalization, resulting in narrower generalization.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing effects of amisulpride on generalization parameters.

claim: Performance on the orientation discrimination task did not differ between groups.
source: Performance (percentage correct) on this task did not differ between groups (two-way, time-by-group ANOVA, main effect of group, F(1,43) = 0.99, P = 0.33) and there was no group-by-time interaction (F(1,43) = 0.42, P = 0.52).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of perceptual discrimination performance.

claim: Perceptual discrimination performance was reliable across time.
source: Moreover, while perceptual discrimination performance was reliable across time (correlation between pre- and post-drug performance, r = 0.52, P < 0.001)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of performance measures.

claim: Perceptual discrimination performance was not related to the width of the estimated generalization coefficients.
source: it was not related to the width of the estimated generalization coefficients (all Ps > 0.38).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between perceptual performance and model parameters.

claim: The effects of amisulpride on generalization cannot be explained by perceptual improvements in orientation discrimination per se.
source: Taken together, this control analysis demonstrates that the effects of amisulpride on generalization cannot be explained by perceptual improvements in orientation discrimination per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment showing no drug effects on perceptual discrimination.

claim: Across the entire group, fMRI signals in the bilateral hippocampus positively correlated with generalized prediction errors.
source: In line with this hypothesis, across the entire group (one sample t-test) we found significant correlations in the bilateral hippocampus (extending into the parahippocampal gyrus, left, x = -30, y = -22, z = -16, t = 6.53, P = 0.001, FWE whole brain corrected; right, x = 33, y = -19, z = -16, t = 7.11, P < 0.001, FWE whole brain corrected, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Similar effects to those in the hippocampus were found in the left amygdala.
source: Similar effects were found in the left amygdala (x = -24, y = -4, z = -19, t = 6.04, P = 0.006, FWE whole brain corrected)
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Similar effects to those in the hippocampus were found in the bilateral middle temporal gyrus.
source: and the bilateral middle temporal gyrus (left, x = -48, y = -73, z = 14, t = 6.41, P = 0.002, FWE whole brain corrected; right, x = 28, y = -64, z = 14, t = 5.57, P = 0.022, FWE whole brain corrected).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: At an uncorrected threshold, a cluster in the mPFC extending into the vmPFC showed prediction error related activity.
source: In addition, supporting recent work highlighting a role for medial (mPFC) and ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) in generalization (Dunsmoor and Paz, 2015; Onat and Buchel, 2015), at an uncorrected threshold of P < 0.001, we found a cluster in the mPFC (x = -3, y = 56, z = 8, t = 4.03) extending into the vmPFC.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and citations to previous research.

claim: Prediction error-related activity in the hippocampus was significantly reduced in the amisulpride group relative to the placebo group.
source: In line with this idea, we found significantly reduced activity in the hippocampus in the amisulpride relative to the placebo group (two-sample t-test, t = -2.12, P = 0.02, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: No significant group differences in prediction error-related activity were observed in the amygdala.
source: No significant group differences were observed in the amygdala (P = 0.43)
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: No significant group differences in prediction error-related activity were observed in the middle temporal gyrus.
source: the middle temporal gyrus (P = 0.31)
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: No significant group differences in prediction error-related activity were observed in the medial PFC.
source: or the medial PFC (P = 0.98).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: The effect of D2R blockade in the hippocampus was significantly stronger than in the mPFC.
source: However, post-hoc analyses directly comparing the effect of the drug in the hippocampus to the drug effect in the other regions (i.e. group-by-region interactions), demonstrated that while the effect of D2R blockade in the hippocampus was significantly stronger than in the mPFC (P = 0.02)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of drug effects across brain regions.

claim: Interactions involving the amygdala and middle temporal gyrus did not reach significance.
source: similar interactions involving the amygdala (P = 0.097) and the middle temporal gyrus (P = 0.127) did not reach significance.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of drug effects across brain regions.

claim: The effects of D2R blockade on similarity-based processing are specific to the hippocampus relative to the mPFC, but not necessarily relative to the amygdala and middle temporal lobe.
source: These data suggest specificity of the effects of D2R blockade on similarity-based processing in the hippocampus relative to the mPFC, but not necessarily relative to the amygdala and middle temporal lobe.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of statistical comparisons across brain regions.

claim: Amisulpride reduced the functional connectivity between the midbrain and the right hippocampus.
source: In line with this prediction, a functional connectivity analysis with the midbrain as a seed region (Figure 8A, see Materials and methods) revealed decreased midbrain connectivity in the right hippocampus (x = 33, y = -19, z = -19, t = 3.68, P = 0.02, FWE small volume corrected, Figure 8B,C)
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Amisulpride reduced the functional connectivity between the midbrain and the left striatum.
source: and the left striatum (x = -9, y = 8, z = -19, t = 4.26, P = 0.001, FWE small volume corrected)
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis.

claim: D2R blockade modulates the functional connectivity between the midbrain and dopaminergic target regions such as the hippocampus and the striatum.
source: This finding suggests that D2R blockade may modulate the functional connectivity between the midbrain and dopaminergic target regions such as the hippocampus and the striatum.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional connectivity results.

claim: Midbrain connectivity with the middle temporal gyrus differed significantly between groups.
source: While connectivity estimates differed significantly between groups in middle temporal gyrus (P = 0.01)
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis.

claim: No drug effects on midbrain connectivity were observed in the amygdala.
source: no drug effects were observed in the amygdala (P = 0.296)
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis.

claim: No drug effects on midbrain connectivity were observed in the mPFC.
source: and the mPFC (P = 0.17).
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Amisulpride-related decreases in midbrain connectivity are relatively specific to the hippocampus.
source: Accordingly, for all regions except the middle temporal gyrus (P = 0.13), the corresponding drug-by-region interactions were significant (all Ps < 0.05), suggesting that amisulpride-related decreases in midbrain connectivity are relatively specific to the hippocampus.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical comparisons of connectivity effects across regions.

claim: Midbrain-hippocampal connectivity was positively correlated with the width of the inhibitory generalization coefficient in the amisulpride group.
source: Specifically, we tested the correlation between midbrain-hippocampal connectivity and the estimated width of generalization coefficients in the amisulpride group. This correlation was significant for the inhibitory generalization coefficient (r = 0.47, P = 0.01, Figure 8D)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Midbrain-hippocampal connectivity was not correlated with the width of the excitatory generalization coefficient in the amisulpride group.
source: but not for the excitatory coefficient (r = 0.18, P = 0.19).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: In a previous dataset, midbrain-hippocampal connectivity was significantly correlated with the inhibitory generalization coefficient.
source: We replicated these findings in our previous data set (Kahnt et al., 2012), showing that midbrain-hippocampal connectivity was significantly correlated with the inhibitory generalization coefficient (r = 0.44, P = 0.036)
evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of a previous dataset.

claim: In a previous dataset, midbrain-hippocampal connectivity was not correlated with the excitatory generalization coefficient.
source: but not with the excitatory coefficient (r = 0.15, P = 0.49).
evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of a previous dataset.

claim: The relationship between connectivity and generalization was not observed for midbrain-striatal connections.
source: Interestingly, this relationship was not observed for midbrain-striatal connections (P > 0.16)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: The relationship between connectivity and generalization was significantly stronger for midbrain-hippocampal compared to midbrain-striatal connectivity.
source: and was significantly stronger for midbrain-hippocampal compared to midbrain-striatal connectivity (Z = 2.31, P = 0.011)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of correlations.

claim: The relation between dopamine and the width of generalization may arise primarily from midbrain-hippocampal connections.
source: suggesting that the relation between dopamine and the width of generalization may arise primarily from midbrain-hippocampal connections.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of connectivity-behavior correlations.

claim: There is a link between dopamine-mediated midbrain-hippocampal coupling and the width of stimulus generalization in humans.
source: In summary, these findings suggest a link between dopamine-mediated midbrain-hippocampal coupling and the width of stimulus generalization in humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of connectivity and behavioral analyses.

claim: The hippocampus contributes to generalization by detecting the relationship between items in memory.
source: Previous empirical and modeling work suggests that the hippocampus contributes to generalization by detecting the relationship between items in memory (Eichenbaum, 1999; Howard et al., 2005; Kumaran and McClelland, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hippocampal function in generalization was thought to only apply to associative forms of generalization involving higher-order relationships, whereas basic stimulus generalization involving perceptual similarity is suggested to be hippocampus-independent.
source: However, this function was thought to only apply to associative forms of generalization involving higher-order relationships, whereas basic stimulus generalization involving perceptual similarity is suggested to be hippocampus-independent (Kumaran, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: The current study provides evidence that the hippocampus is involved in stimulus generalization.
source: Opposing this view, here we provide evidence that the hippocampus is involved in stimulus generalization.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing hippocampal involvement.

claim: Hippocampal similarity computations are not restricted to detecting higher-order relationships among stimuli but can also exploit the perceptual similarity between stimuli to establish meaningful relationships.
source: Accordingly, our findings suggest that hippocampal similarity computations are not restricted to detecting higher-order relationships among stimuli as previously thought, but can also exploit the perceptual similarity between stimuli to establish meaningful relationships.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The hippocampus may not be necessary for stimulus generalization per se, but it facilitates generalization by allowing a flexible modulation of its width.
source: While the hippocampus may not be necessary for stimulus generalization per se, our data suggest that it facilitates generalization by allowing a flexible modulation of its width.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental findings.

claim: Two alternative accounts suggest that the relationship among stimuli is established by the hippocampus either during encoding via overlapping neural codes or at the time of retrieval by means of recurrent similarity computations that are based on separated neural codes.
source: Two alternative accounts suggest that the relationship among stimuli is established by the hippocampus either during encoding via overlapping neural codes (Eichenbaum, 1999; Howard et al., 2005), or at the time of retrieval by means of recurrent similarity computations that are based on separated neural codes (Kumaran and McClelland, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The encoding account has received empirical support from studies showing that hippocampal activity during encoding is related to transfer performance at test.
source: The former proposal has received empirical support from studies showing that hippocampal activity during encoding is related to transfer performance at test (Shohamy and Wagner, 2008; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous empirical studies.

claim: The computational model assumes that reward predictions are generalized and integrated during test.
source: In contrast, in line with the second account, our model assumes that reward predictions are generalized and integrated during test (Pearce, 1987).
evidence: This is based on the structure of the computational model and citation to previous modeling work.

claim: The model is mathematically equivalent to a model in which generalization occurs at encoding.
source: It should be noted though that this model is mathematically equivalent to a model in which generalization occurs at encoding (Kahnt et al., 2012), and thus, the model alone does not provide evidence for either account.
evidence: This is based on mathematical properties of the model and citation to previous work.

claim: Only if generalization occurs at retrieval can the width of generalization be modulated after encoding has occurred.
source: However, only if generalization occurs at retrieval can the width of generalization be modulated after encoding has occurred, and thus, our results are only compatible with a retrieval-based account of generalization.
evidence: This is inferred from the logic of the experimental design.

claim: The pharmacological manipulation provides evidence that stimulus generalization occurs – at least in part – at retrieval.
source: Specifically, because dopamine receptor blockade modulated generalization gradients during test, without affecting additional learning, our pharmacological manipulation provides evidence that stimulus generalization occurs – at least in part – at retrieval.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing drug effects at test but not during training.

claim: Direct dopaminergic innervation from the midbrain to the hippocampus is present and functionally relevant for memory stabilization.
source: While the presence of dopamine receptors in the hippocampus is undisputed, it is worth keeping in mind that although direct dopaminergic innervation from the midbrain to the hippocampus is present (Gasbarri et al., 1994) and functionally relevant for memory stabilization (McNamara et al., 2014), this pathway is not very strong (Mingote et al., 2015; Swanson, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical and functional studies.

claim: The dopaminergic pathway from the midbrain to the hippocampus is not very strong.
source: While the presence of dopamine receptors in the hippocampus is undisputed, it is worth keeping in mind that although direct dopaminergic innervation from the midbrain to the hippocampus is present (Gasbarri et al., 1994) and functionally relevant for memory stabilization (McNamara et al., 2014), this pathway is not very strong (Mingote et al., 2015; Swanson, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Some of the hippocampal dopamine may be co-released from noradrenergic neurons.
source: Moreover, it is conceivable that some of the hippocampal dopamine is co-released from noradrenergic neurons, in which it may not have been completely metabolized.
evidence: This is speculated based on known neurobiological mechanisms.

claim: Reduced activity of hippocampal D2R decreases the extent to which reward associations generalize across stimuli.
source: As such, our data is in line with the idea that reduced activity of hippocampal D2R decreases the extent to which reward associations generalize across stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Enhanced dopaminergic activity in the hippocampus may increase the width of generalization.
source: By extension, enhanced dopaminergic activity in the hippocampus may increase the width of generalization.
evidence: This is speculated based on the inverse of the observed drug effect.

claim: Dopamine release in the hippocampus could increase the likelihood that ensemble patterns representing similar stimuli are activated, which would effectively lower the threshold for similarity detection and facilitate generalization.
source: More specifically, dopamine release in the hippocampus could increase the likelihood that ensemble patterns representing similar stimuli are activated, which would effectively lower the threshold for similarity detection, and, by broadening the range of stimuli for which reward predictions are taken into account, facilitate generalization.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation based on the findings.

claim: Reduced levels of dopamine would decrease the likelihood of ensemble pattern activation, increase the threshold for similarity detection, and reduce generalization.
source: Conversely, reduced levels of dopamine would decrease the likelihood of ensemble pattern activation, increase the threshold for similarity detection, and, by enhancing fine-tuned discrimination, reduce generalization.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation based on the findings.

claim: Dopamine may flexibly adjust generalization during retrieval.
source: This provides a simple neurobiological mechanism by which dopamine may flexibly adjust generalization during retrieval.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanism.

claim: Tonic dopamine levels may play an enabling role in generalization, similar to their enabling effects on movements.
source: We speculate that tonic dopamine levels, similar to their enabling effects on movements (Schultz, 2007), play an enabling role in generalization.
evidence: This is speculated based on analogy to known dopamine functions and citation to previous work.

claim: In situations where dopamine transmission is high, such as in novel environments, elevated levels of dopamine may not only support memory formation but also broaden generalization and thereby facilitate exploratory behavior.
source: For instance, in situations where dopamine transmission is high, such as in novel environments (Ihalainen et al., 1999; Lisman and Grace, 2005), elevated levels of dopamine may not only support memory formation (Shohamy and Adcock, 2010), but also broaden generalization and thereby facilitate exploratory behavior.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings and citations to previous research.

claim: D2R blockade reduced generalization coefficients for both excitatory and inhibitory associations, albeit less reliably for inhibitory associations.
source: Of note, although D2R blockade reduced generalization coefficients for both excitatory and inhibitory associations (albeit less reliably)
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results.

claim: Midbrain-hippocampal connectivity was only correlated with the width of the inhibitory coefficient.
source: midbrain-hippocampal connectivity was only correlated with the width of the inhibitory coefficient.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Only the effects of D2R blockade on the inhibitory coefficient are mediated via a modulation of midbrain-hippocampal connectivity, whereas the effects on the excitatory coefficient are mediated via a different mechanism.
source: This raises the possibility that only the effects of D2R blockade on the inhibitory coefficient are mediated via a modulation of midbrain-hippocampal connectivity, whereas the effects on the excitatory coefficient are mediated via a different, yet to be explored, mechanism.
evidence: This is speculated based on the pattern of correlations.

claim: The dissociation between inhibitory and excitatory generalization coefficients is in line with previous results suggesting that chlorpromazine specifically reduces the strength of inhibitory associations in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The dissociation between inhibitory and excitatory generalization coefficients is in line with the interpretation of previous results suggesting that administration of chlorpromazine, a nonspecific dopamine receptor antagonist, specifically reduces the strength of inhibitory associations in a dose-dependent manner (Lyons et al., 1973b; Terrace, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Generalization involving appetitive and aversive outcomes may involve different mechanisms.
source: Moreover, it adds to previous findings indicating that generalization involving appetitive and aversive outcomes may involve different mechanisms (Schechtman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The current experiment suggests an association between dopamine and the width of generalization in the hippocampus.
source: Specifically, the current experiment suggests an association between dopamine and the width of generalization in the hippocampus
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The current experiment dissociates effects of generalization during retrieval vs. encoding.
source: and dissociates effects of generalization during retrieval vs. encoding, which could not be achieved with the previous design.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design.

claim: In the current study, prediction errors correlate primarily with activity in the hippocampus, whereas the previous study identified prediction error related activity primarily in the ventral striatum.
source: However, whereas here we find that prediction errors correlate primarily with activity in the hippocampus, the previous study identified prediction error related activity primarily in the ventral striatum.
evidence: This is a comparison between current and previous findings.

claim: In the previous study, functional connectivity between the striatum and the hippocampus was related to the modeled generalization coefficients, whereas current results suggest a facilitating role of midbrain-hippocampal connections.
source: Also, in the previous study functional connectivity between the striatum and the hippocampus was related to the modeled generalization coefficients, whereas our current results suggest a facilitating role of midbrain-hippocampal connections.
evidence: This is a comparison between current and previous findings.

claim: The previous design consisted of multiple alternating training and testing blocks, all conducted within one session on a single day, whereas in the current study, training and test did not alternate but were conducted in distinct sessions that were separated by a 24 hr delay.
source: Most importantly, the previous design consisted of multiple alternating training and testing blocks, all conducted within one session on a single day, whereas in the current study, training and test did not alternate but were conducted in distinct sessions that were separated by a 24 hr delay.
evidence: This is a description of methodological differences between studies.

claim: In the 2012 study, CS-outcome associations were deterministic (100% contingency), whereas the current experiment involved a 50% reinforcement schedule.
source: Moreover, in the 2012 study, CS-outcome associations were deterministic (100% contingency), whereas the current experiment involved a 50% reinforcement schedule in order to slow down extinction during test.
evidence: This is a description of methodological differences between studies.

claim: Design differences between studies could have shifted the primary focus of generalization-related processing from the striatum to the hippocampus.

claim: The study proposes a neurobiological mechanism for the control of stimulus generalization, in which midbrain dopamine changes similarity computations in the hippocampus, resulting in altered generalization gradients.
source: In conclusion, here we propose a neurobiological mechanism for the control of stimulus generalization, in which midbrain dopamine changes similarity computations in the hippocampus, resulting in altered generalization gradients.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental findings.

claim: The width of stimulus generalization is not hard-wired but flexible, and can change under pharmacological interventions.
source: As such, our results demonstrate that the width of stimulus generalization is not hard-wired but flexible, and can change under pharmacological interventions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing drug effects on generalization.

claim: The results have important clinical implications for a number of neuropsychiatric disorders in which generalization is disrupted.
source: Accordingly, our results have important clinical implications for a number of neuropsychiatric disorders in which generalization is disrupted.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings and their potential applications.

claim: Aberrant generalization is implicated in depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia.
source: Specifically, aberrant generalization is implicated in depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia (Buss and Daniell, 1967; Gotlib and Joormann, 2010; Lissek et al., 2014b; Shohamy et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Blocking D2R activity may provide a potential treatment of overgeneralization in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: and our findings indicate that blocking D2R activity may provide a potential treatment of overgeneralization in these disorders.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings and their potential clinical applications.

claim: Subjects were assigned to groups in a double-blind and pseudo-random fashion.
source: Subjects were assigned to one of three groups in a double-blind and pseudo-random fashion: amisulpride-placebo (AP), placebo-amisulpride (PA), and placebo-placebo (PP).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Seven subjects were excluded because they either failed to acquire stimulus-outcome associations during discrimination training or failed to follow instructions.
source: A total of seven subjects was excluded because they either failed to acquire stimulus-outcome associations during the discrimination training on day one (performance <60%, 4 subjects) or because they failed to follow instructions on day two (3 subjects).
evidence: This is a description of the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Groups did not differ significantly in number, average age, or average weight.
source: Groups did not differ significantly in number (PA: N = 25, PP: N=21, chi-square = 0.348, P = 0.56), average age, (PA: 22.72 years ± 2.17 SD, PP: 22.19 years ± 1.83 SD; t = 0.88, P = 0.38), and average weight (PA: 75.04 kg ± 7.89 SD, PP: 75.48 kg ± 10.92 SD; t = -0.03, P = 0.98).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons of demographic variables.

claim: Subjects were not aware of whether they received placebo or amisulpride on both days.
source: Moreover, subjects were not aware of whether they received placebo or amisulpride on both days as assessed by a post experimental questionnaire (day I, chi-square = 0.49, P = 0.48, day II: chi-square = 0.29, P = 0.60).
evidence: This is supported by post-experimental questionnaire data.

claim: The study was approved by the Cantonal Ethics Review Board of Zurich.
source: The study was approved by the Cantonal Ethics Review Board of Zurich, and subjects provided informed consent to participate.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The CS+ was paired with reward and no reward in 50% of the trials, whereas the CS− was always paired with no reward.
source: The CS+ was paired with reward and no reward in 50% of the trials, whereas the CS− was always paired with no reward.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

source: The outcome was independent of the correctness of the behavioral response

claim: The generalization test was performed in extinction, with no outcomes shown for all orientations.
source: Importantly, the test was performed in extinction, i.e. no outcomes were shown for all orientations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The extinction design ensured that subjects made motor responses to all stimuli and allowed observation of reward prediction error responses to all orientations independent of potential confounds.
source: This design ensured that subjects made motor responses to all stimuli and thus allowed us to observe reward prediction error responses to all orientations independent of potential confounds attributable to reward feedback, different visual stimulation, and different cognitive or motor demands.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: Cue-evoked activity in the calcarine sulcus did not differ between groups.
source: Cue-related activity in an anatomical mask of the calcarine sulcus (AAL) did not differ between groups (t = -0.80, P = 0.42), suggesting that amisulpride did not unspecifically affect the BOLD response.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Amisulpride did not unspecifically affect the BOLD response.
source: Cue-related activity in an anatomical mask of the calcarine sulcus (AAL) did not differ between groups (t = -0.80, P = 0.42), suggesting that amisulpride did not unspecifically affect the BOLD response.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of group differences in visual cortex activity.

claim: Previous studies found no differences in visually evoked activity between amisulpride and placebo.
source: This is in line with previous studies that found no differences in visually evoked activity between amisulpride and placebo (Jocham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There was a trend-level group difference in RT, with slower responding in amisulpride compared to placebo.
source: Although amisulpride is generally known to not alter RT (Jocham et al., 2011; Rosenzweig et al., 2002), we found a trend-level group difference in RT (t = 1.83, P = 0.074), with slower responding in amisulpride (mean RT ± SEM = 816 ± 16.6) compared to placebo (mean RT ± SEM = 770 ± 18.5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of reaction time data.

claim: All group comparisons remained significant when RT was included as a covariate in the statistical models.
source: Importantly, all group comparisons remained significant when RT was included as a covariate in the statistical models, suggesting that non-significant differences in RT did not confound the imaging results.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis controlling for RT.
